cards.q: What are stereoisomers?
cards.a: Compounds with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of their atoms in space.
cards.why: E/Z isomerism and optical isomerism are the two kinds of stereoisomerism at A-level.

cards.q: What is a chiral centre (an asymmetric carbon atom)?
cards.a: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups.
cards.why: A molecule with one chiral centre cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, so it has two optical isomers.

cards.q: What are enantiomers (optical isomers)?
cards.a: A pair of stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
cards.why: They exist because the molecule contains a chiral centre.

cards.q: What does it mean to say a molecule is chiral?
cards.a: It cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, however it is turned.
cards.why: Your left and right hands are the everyday example: mirror images that never line up exactly.

cards.q: What does “non-superimposable” mean when describing two enantiomers?
cards.a: However one molecule is rotated, it can never be placed on the other so that every atom lines up with the same atom.
cards.why: Rotating the molecule never helps; only swapping two of the groups on the chiral centre turns one enantiomer into the other.

cards.q: How do the two enantiomers of a compound differ in their effect on plane-polarised light?
cards.a: They rotate the plane of plane-polarised light by the same angle but in opposite directions.
cards.why: One rotates the plane clockwise, the other anticlockwise.

cards.q: What is meant by optical activity?
cards.a: The ability of a single optical isomer to rotate the plane of polarisation of plane-polarised monochromatic light.
cards.why: A substance that rotates the plane is optically active; one that does not is optically inactive.

cards.q: Apart from their effect on plane-polarised light, how do the physical and chemical properties of two enantiomers compare?
cards.a: They are the same: same melting and boiling points, same density, same reactions with ordinary (non-chiral) reagents.
cards.why: They can behave differently with other chiral molecules, such as enzymes and receptors in the body.

cards.q: Describe how you could show that a solution of sucrose is optically active.
cards.a: Pass plane-polarised light through the solution and show that the plane of polarisation is rotated.
marks: Pass monochromatic light through a polarising filter to give plane-polarised light.
Pass the plane-polarised light through a tube of the sucrose solution.
Turn a second polarising filter (the analyser) until the light seen is at its brightest (or darkest).
Compare with a tube of pure water: the angle has changed, so the plane of polarisation has been rotated.

cards.q: Why is monochromatic light used to measure optical activity?
cards.a: The angle through which the plane is rotated depends on the wavelength of the light, so a single wavelength gives one definite angle.
cards.why: Sodium lamps (589 nm) are traditionally used for this.

cards.q: Does butan-2-ol have a chiral centre? If so, identify it.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of butan-2-ol: a four-carbon zigzag chain with an OH group on the second carbon.

cards.a: Yes: carbon 2, which is bonded to \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\).
cards.why: Four different groups on one carbon, so butan-2-ol has two enantiomers.

cards.q: Does propan-2-ol have a chiral centre?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of propan-2-ol: a three-carbon chain with an OH group on the middle carbon.

cards.a: No. Carbon 2 carries two identical \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) groups.
cards.why: A chiral centre needs four different groups; two the same means the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image.

cards.q: Does 3-methylpentane have a chiral centre?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 3-methylpentane: a five-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle carbon.

cards.a: No. Carbon 3 carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and two identical ethyl groups.
cards.why: Look along each branch in full: here two of the four groups are the same, so the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image.

cards.q: Does 3-methylhexane have a chiral centre? If so, which carbon?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 3-methylhexane: a six-carbon zigzag chain with a methyl branch on the third carbon.

cards.a: Yes: carbon 3, bonded to \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{7}}\).
cards.why: An alkane can be chiral: the four groups need not contain different elements.

cards.q: Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) forms when milk sours and when cassava is fermented to make garri. Does it have a chiral centre?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid: a COOH group and a CH3 group on a carbon that also carries an OH group.

cards.a: Yes: carbon 2, bonded to \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{COOH}\).
cards.why: So lactic acid exists as two enantiomers.

cards.q: Does 2-methylbutan-1-ol have a chiral centre? If so, which carbon?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-methylbutan-1-ol: a four-carbon chain with OH on carbon 1 and a methyl branch on carbon 2.

cards.a: Yes: carbon 2, bonded to \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{2}OH}\).
cards.why: The carbon carrying the OH group is not the chiral centre here: it has two hydrogens.

cards.q: Which of these amino acids has a chiral centre: glycine or alanine? (The figure shows alanine.)

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of alanine, 2-aminopropanoic acid: a carbon carrying NH2, CH3 and COOH groups.

cards.a: Alanine. Its carbon 2 carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{COOH}\). Glycine’s carbon 2 carries two hydrogens, so it is not chiral.
cards.why: Glycine is the only common amino acid that is not optically active.

cards.q: Ibuprofen, a common painkiller, is sold as a racemic mixture. Identify its chiral centre.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of ibuprofen: a benzene ring with a 2-methylpropyl group on one side and a CH(CH3)COOH group on the opposite side.

cards.a: The carbon joined to the ring, which carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{COOH}\) and the benzene ring.
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{CH}\) in the 2-methylpropyl group is not chiral: it carries two identical \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) groups.

cards.q: One enantiomer of carvone smells of spearmint and the other of caraway seeds. Identify the chiral centre, and suggest why the two smell different.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of carvone: a six-membered ring containing a C=O group and a C=C bond, with a methyl group and an isopropenyl group, CH3C=CH2, on the ring.

cards.a: The ring carbon carrying the isopropenyl group (and an H). The smell receptors in the nose are chiral, so each enantiomer fits them differently.
cards.why: The two paths round the ring from that carbon are different, so the ring counts as two different groups.

cards.q: Can a carbon atom in a C=C double bond be a chiral centre?
cards.a: No. It is bonded to only three groups, and the groups round it lie in one plane.
cards.why: A chiral centre needs four different groups arranged tetrahedrally.

cards.q: True or false: a chiral centre must be bonded to four different atoms.
cards.a: False. It must be bonded to four different groups.
cards.why: In butan-2-ol, carbon 2 is bonded to two carbon atoms, but one is part of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and the other part of \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\): different groups.

cards.q: In a 3D drawing of a chiral centre, what do a plain line, a solid wedge and a hashed wedge each show?

figure.alt: One enantiomer of butan-2-ol: the central carbon has H up and CH3 to the lower left on plain lines, OH on a solid wedge to the right and C2H5 on a hashed wedge pointing down.

cards.a:
Plain line: a bond in the plane of the paper.
Solid wedge: a bond coming towards you.
Hashed wedge: a bond going away from you, behind the paper.
cards.why: Two bonds in the plane, one forward and one back show the tetrahedral shape round the carbon.

cards.q: Draw the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid) in 3D.
cards.a: Draw one 3D structure, then its reflection in a mirror placed between them.

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid either side of a dashed mirror line. Each has OH up and H on a hashed bond down; on the left CH3 is in the plane and COOH on a wedge to the right, and on the right these are reflected.

cards.why: The mirror swaps left and right but not front and back, so wedges stay wedges and hashes stay hashes.

cards.q: Draw the two enantiomers of butan-2-ol in 3D.
cards.a: The chiral carbon carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\); draw one arrangement and its mirror image.

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of butan-2-ol either side of a dashed mirror line: each has H up, C2H5 on a hashed bond down, and CH3 in the plane and OH on a wedge, reflected left to right.

cards.why: A mark scheme needs a clear tetrahedral shape (two plain bonds, one wedge, one hash) and the two drawings to be mirror images.

cards.q: Draw the two enantiomers of alanine, 2-aminopropanoic acid, in 3D.
cards.a: The chiral carbon carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{COOH}\).

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of alanine either side of a dashed mirror line: each has H up and NH2 on a hashed bond down, with CH3 in the plane and COOH on a wedge, reflected left to right.

cards.why: Almost all amino acids in proteins are one enantiomer only, because the enzymes that make them are chiral.

cards.q: Draw the two enantiomers of 2-bromobutane in 3D.
cards.a: The chiral carbon carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\).

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of 2-bromobutane either side of a dashed mirror line: each has H up and Br on a hashed bond down, with C2H5 in the plane and CH3 on a wedge, reflected left to right.

cards.why: Any arrangement is fine for the first drawing; the second must be its mirror image.

cards.q: Draw the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, the product of ethanal with HCN.
cards.a: The chiral carbon carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{CN}\).

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanenitrile either side of a dashed mirror line: each has OH up and H on a hashed bond down, with CH3 in the plane and CN on a wedge, reflected left to right.

cards.why: Write the nitrile group as NC when it is on the left, so the bond is clearly to the carbon.

cards.q: Are these two drawings the same molecule or a pair of enantiomers?

figure.alt: Two 3D drawings of 2-chlorobutane side by side. Left: H up, CH3 in the plane, Cl on a wedge, C2H5 on a hash. Right: the same, except Cl and CH3 have swapped places, so CH3 is on the wedge and Cl is in the plane.

cards.a: Enantiomers. Swapping any two groups on a chiral centre gives the other enantiomer.
cards.why: Swapping two groups once inverts the centre; swapping twice gets back to the same molecule.

cards.q: Why is the structural formula of a compound such as butan-2-ol not enough to show which enantiomer is meant?
cards.a: Both enantiomers have the same structural formula, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{2}CH_{3}}\), and the same displayed formula. Only a 3D drawing (with wedges) shows the arrangement in space.
cards.why: Enantiomers differ only in how the four groups are arranged round the chiral centre.

cards.q: What is a racemic mixture (racemate)?
cards.a: A mixture of equal amounts of the two enantiomers of a compound.
cards.why: Also called a racemate; it is optically inactive.

cards.q: Explain why a racemic mixture is optically inactive.
cards.a: The rotations caused by the two enantiomers cancel out.
marks: A racemate contains equal amounts (equal concentrations) of the two enantiomers.
Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by the same angle in opposite directions.
The rotations cancel, so there is no overall rotation.

cards.q: Explain how a racemic mixture forms when a reaction goes through a planar intermediate or a planar reactant group.

figure.alt: Ethanal drawn with its planar C=O group: O up, CH3 on a wedge and H on a hashed bond. A cyanide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon from the left face and another from the right face.

text.t: equal chance of attack from either face

cards.a: The nucleophile is equally likely to attack either face of the planar group, so each enantiomer forms in equal amounts.
marks: The group attacked is planar (trigonal planar), such as a \(\mathrm{C=O}\) group or a carbocation.
The nucleophile can attack from above or below the plane (from either side).
Attack from each side is equally likely.
So the two enantiomers form in equal amounts: a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive.

cards.q: Ethanal reacts with KCN followed by dilute acid. Draw the two products that form, and say how much of each forms.
cards.a: Equal amounts of the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanenitrile: a racemic mixture.

answerFigure.alt: The two enantiomers of 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, mirror images either side of a dashed line, formed in equal amounts.

cards.why: The product mixture does not rotate plane-polarised light.

cards.q: When HBr adds to but-1-ene, the 2-bromobutane formed is optically inactive. Explain why.

figure.alt: The secondary carbocation formed when HBr adds to but-1-ene: the positive carbon carries H, CH3 and C2H5 in one plane. A bromide ion can attack from the left face or from the right face.

cards.a: The secondary carbocation is planar, so bromide attacks both faces equally, giving a racemate.
marks: The major product forms via the secondary carbocation \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH^{+}CH_{2}CH_{3}}\).
The carbocation is planar about the positive carbon.
\(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) attacks from either side with equal probability.
Equal amounts of the two enantiomers of 2-bromobutane form: a racemic mixture, so the rotations cancel.

cards.q: Propanone reacts with HCN to give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Is the product a racemic mixture?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile: a central carbon carrying two methyl groups, an OH group and a C≡N group.

cards.a: No. The product has no chiral centre: its central carbon carries two \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) groups. Only one compound forms.
cards.why: A symmetrical ketone gives an achiral product; an aldehyde or an unsymmetrical ketone gives a racemate.

cards.q: Lactic acid made in muscle cells is a single enantiomer, but lactic acid made in the laboratory from ethanal (by adding HCN, then hydrolysing) is optically inactive. Explain the difference.
cards.a: The enzyme in muscle is chiral, so it makes only one enantiomer. In the laboratory, \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) attacks the planar \(\mathrm{C=O}\) of ethanal from both sides equally, giving a racemic mixture.
cards.why: Nature’s catalysts are chiral; ordinary reagents are not, so they cannot favour one face.

cards.q: A drug molecule has one chiral centre, and only one enantiomer is pharmacologically active. Suggest why manufacturers try to make the single enantiomer rather than the racemate.
cards.a: Half of a racemate is the inactive (or possibly harmful) enantiomer.
marks: Only one enantiomer fits the chiral target (receptor or enzyme) in the body.
The other enantiomer may have no effect, or may cause side effects.
A racemate means a double dose is needed for the same effect.
Separating a racemate is difficult and costly, so syntheses using chiral catalysts or enzymes are preferred.

cards.q: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane is hydrolysed by aqueous hydroxide ions by an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism. Is the butan-2-ol formed optically active? Explain.

figure.alt: SN2 on one enantiomer of 2-bromobutane: the hydroxide lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite the bromine, the C–Br bond breaks, and the other three groups flip over like an umbrella, giving one enantiomer of butan-2-ol.

cards.a: Yes. Attack from the side opposite the bromine inverts the arrangement, giving a single enantiomer of the product.
marks: In \(\mathrm{S_{N}2}\), \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) attacks the \(\delta+\) carbon from the side opposite the C–Br bond, in one step.
The other three groups are pushed through, like an umbrella turning inside out: the configuration is inverted.
Every molecule reacts the same way, so only one enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms.
So the product is optically active.

cards.q: A single enantiomer of 3-bromo-3-methylhexane is hydrolysed by an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. Explain why the product is optically inactive.

figure.alt: The planar carbocation from 3-bromo-3-methylhexane, with C2H5 up and the CH3 and C3H7 groups in the same plane; one hydroxide ion attacks from the left face and another from the right face, each with equal probability.

text.t: equal chance of attack from either face

cards.a: The planar carbocation is attacked equally from both sides, giving a racemic mixture.
marks: In \(\mathrm{S_{N}1}\), the C–Br bond breaks first to form a tertiary carbocation.
The carbocation is planar about the positive carbon.
\(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) (or water) attacks from either side with equal probability.
Equal amounts of both enantiomers form: a racemic mixture, with no overall rotation.

cards.q: An optically active halogenoalkane is hydrolysed. The product mixture does not rotate plane-polarised light. Which mechanism is likely: S<sub>N</sub>1 or S<sub>N</sub>2?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{S_{N}1}\): a planar carbocation intermediate is attacked from both sides, giving a racemate.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{S_{N}2}\) would give a single, inverted enantiomer, which would rotate the light.

cards.q: An optically active halogenoalkane is hydrolysed and the product rotates plane-polarised light. Which mechanism does this support, and why?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{S_{N}2}\): one-step attack from the side opposite the halogen gives a single enantiomer of the product.
cards.why: There is no planar intermediate, so a racemate cannot form.

cards.q: A single enantiomer of a secondary halogenoalkane is hydrolysed. The product rotates plane-polarised light, but by less than the pure product enantiomer would. Suggest what this shows.
cards.a: Both mechanisms are happening: some molecules react by \(\mathrm{S_{N}2}\) (one enantiomer) and some by \(\mathrm{S_{N}1}\) (a racemate).
cards.why: Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by either mechanism, so partial loss of optical activity is common.

cards.q: True or false: because S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts the arrangement round the carbon, the product must rotate plane-polarised light in the opposite direction to the reactant.
cards.a: False. The product is a different compound, so its direction and angle of rotation cannot be predicted from the reactant’s.
cards.why: What the data show is only whether the product is optically active (SN2) or a racemate (SN1).

cards.q: True or false: a racemic mixture is optically inactive because it contains no chiral molecules.
cards.a: False. Every molecule in it is chiral; there are equal amounts of the two enantiomers, so their rotations cancel.
cards.why: An achiral compound is optically inactive for a different reason: it has no chiral centre.

cards.q: True or false: the two enantiomers of butan-2-ol have different boiling points.
cards.a: False. Enantiomers have identical boiling points, melting points and densities.
cards.why: Their intermolecular forces are identical; only their effect on plane-polarised light (and on other chiral molecules) differs.

cards.q: True or false: any sample of a compound with a chiral centre is optically active.
cards.a: False. A racemic mixture of the compound is optically inactive.
cards.why: Only a sample with more of one enantiomer than the other rotates plane-polarised light.

cards.q: True or false: enantiomers are structural isomers.
cards.a: False. They are stereoisomers: same structural formula, different arrangement in space.
cards.why: Structural isomers have different structural formulae (different chain, position or functional group).

cards.q: How many optical isomers does a molecule with one chiral centre have?
cards.a: Two: a pair of enantiomers.
cards.why: At A-level only molecules with a single chiral centre are studied.
